strengths: MaskSub is a simple, technically coherent training method: the shared network receives label supervision on full images and matches detached predictions on masked images. It adds no inference parameters or computation. The supported practical contribution makes the balance favor weak acceptance despite reservations about novelty and interpretation.

The main ImageNet results consistently improve strong supervised baselines. Table 1 reports gains of 0.6–0.7 percentage points across four ViT sizes at 400 epochs and 0.3–0.5 points at 800 epochs. Table A.13 provides supporting three-run statistics; for example, ViT-B achieves 84.08 ± 0.02 versus the reported baseline of 83.46 ± 0.04.

The paper meaningfully addresses additional training cost. Table 8 compares ViT-B MaskSub at 84.1% and 25 GPU-days against longer baseline training at 83.7% and 26 GPU-days. Table 9 also shows a favorable comparison with CoSub: 84.1% at 25.1 GPU-days versus 83.9% at 35.3 GPU-days. These controls support usefulness beyond simply spending more computation.

Evaluation breadth is a substantial strength. Results cover ResNet and Swin, several pretrained-model finetuning recipes, classification transfer, ADE20K segmentation, COCO detection, and distribution shifts. For example, ViT-B ImageNet-A accuracy improves from 36.8% to 41.9% in Table A.4, while segmentation gains reach 0.6 mIoU in Table 10. The contribution therefore extends beyond ImageNet validation accuracy.

The appendix provides useful ablations of distillation, masking ratios, loss weights, and alternative drop regularizers, together with repeated runs for several experiments. Tables A.7–A.8 indicate tolerance to a range of hyperparameters. The concise algorithm, detailed vision training configurations, and provided code link support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is more limited than the framing suggests. Equation (3) is prediction-consistency training: cross-entropy to a detached teacher distribution has the same student gradient as KL divergence to that distribution. Consequently, Section 2's distinction between MaskSub's 'distillation loss' and UDA's 'consistency loss' does not establish a fundamentally different objective. The strongest contribution is the efficient masked-view construction and its empirical integration into supervised recipes.

The proposed mechanism is only partially established. Figure 2 supports smaller early sub-branch gradients and improved optimization, but does not establish the claim that masking is effectively applied exclusively to successfully predicted examples. Every example participates, and an incorrect, confident teacher can supply a strong target. Likewise, worse loss and accuracy under direct masking demonstrate difficulty under the selected recipe, rather than proving general training instability.

Benefits are not uniform across applications. In Table A.10, adding MaskSub during finetuning to the MaskSub-pretrained ViT-B reduces CIFAR-100 accuracy from 91.89% to 89.55%, well beyond the reported variability. Section 4.2 also explicitly states that CLIP finetuning has the same best-checkpoint performance as the baseline, despite improved final-epoch results. These findings qualify the claims of broadly consistent improvements without task-specific adjustment.

Evidence for the smaller improvements is less conclusive than for the principal ViT experiments. BEiTv2's 0.1-point gains and COCO's 0.2–0.3-point gains lack corresponding repeated-run uncertainty. Some transfer improvements are small relative to the reported standard deviations. Furthermore, several comparisons in Table 6 use different training recipes or architectures, so they cannot establish the broad claim that previous self-distillation methods are incompatible with strong recipes; the matched comparisons provide stronger evidence.

There are narrower reproducibility and presentation issues. The GLUE description omits task-specific optimization settings and checkpoint-selection details. Table A.6 does not clearly specify what objective replaces the removed KD loss. Minor reporting corrections include the duplicated CIFAR-100 column heading in Table 7 and the blanket 50% masking statement despite the documented 15% BERT setting. These correctable issues are secondary to the scientific reservations above.

strengths: MaskSub provides a simple, technically coherent training recipe: the shared model receives label supervision on full inputs and matches detached predictions on masked inputs. It adds no inference parameters, and token removal reduces the cost of the auxiliary branch.

The main ImageNet results convincingly demonstrate improvements over a strong baseline. Table 1 reports gains of 0.6–0.7 percentage points over DeiT-III at 400 epochs across model sizes. Repeated runs strengthen this evidence: Table A.13 reports ViT-B improving from 83.46±0.04 to 84.08±0.02.

Comparisons at matched training cost address an important alternative explanation for the gains. Table 8 reports ViT-B reaching 84.1% in 25 GPU days versus 83.7% in 26 GPU days for longer baseline training. Table 9 also demonstrates a favorable accuracy–cost tradeoff against CoSub.

Evaluation breadth supports practical usefulness across architectures and training settings, including ResNet, Swin, pretrained-model finetuning, robustness benchmarks, and downstream vision tasks. ADE20K improves by 0.4–0.6 mIoU, while the supplementary COCO experiment improves box and mask AP. CLIP pretraining additionally improves zero-shot ImageNet accuracy from 33.5% to 37.6%.

The appendix contains substantive ablations and implementation details. Table A.6 shows that removing distillation substantially reduces the benefit; other experiments examine masking ratios, loss weights, and alternative regularizers. Pseudocode, detailed recipes, selected three-run statistics, and a code link support reproducibility. These empirical and practical contributions provide a strong basis for weak acceptance.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is narrower than the manuscript claims. With the teacher distribution detached, Equation (3) has the same student gradient as KL consistency between full and augmented views. Consequently, the distinction from UDA based on 'distillation loss' versus 'consistency loss' is not mathematically substantive. The contribution is principally the effective integration of masking and consistency training into supervised recipes.

The automatic difficulty-control explanation is suggestive rather than established. Equation (3) supervises every example, including confidently incorrect teacher predictions; it does not apply masking exclusively to successfully classified examples as the text suggests. The loss and gradient plots support improved optimization, but do not establish that this particular mechanism causes the gains or distinguish excessive regularization from training instability.

The claimed generality needs qualification. In Table A.10, adding MaskSub during finetuning decreases ViT-B CIFAR-100 accuracy from 91.89% to 89.55%. Section 4.2 also states that CLIP's best checkpoint accuracy is unchanged, so the reported improvement concerns the final checkpoint. These are meaningful limits on the claim of consistently improved performance.

Some comparative claims are less secure than the main ViT results. Several self-distillation baselines in Table 6 use different training recipes, and small gains such as BEiTv2's 0.1 percentage point improvement lack reported variability. Hierarchical architectures require approximately twice the training computation, and equivalent-budget evidence is not provided for every extension, including Swin.

Presentation issues are secondary but should be corrected: Table 7 labels both CIFAR columns as CIFAR100, and ViT-H patch-size labels alternate between /14 and /16. These inconsistencies complicate interpretation without undermining the central empirical findings.

strengths: MaskSub provides a simple, technically coherent method for incorporating strong masking into supervised learning. A masked pass learns from stopped-gradient predictions of an unmasked pass through the same network, adding no model parameters or inference cost.

The central empirical contribution is well supported. Table 1 reports 0.3–0.7 percentage-point improvements over strong DeiT-III recipes across model sizes and training lengths. Table A.13 reports ViT-B accuracy of 84.08 ± 0.02 versus 83.46 ± 0.04 for the baseline, supporting an improvement beyond reported run variability.

The paper meaningfully addresses training cost. Table 8 reports 84.1% for MaskSub using 25 GPU-days versus 83.7% for longer baseline training using 26 GPU-days. Table 9 also shows a favorable accuracy–cost tradeoff against CoSub. These comparisons establish practical value under comparable resource budgets.

Evaluation is broad and relevant to computer vision: MAE/BEiTv2 finetuning, ResNet and Swin training, classification transfer, ADE20K segmentation, COCO detection, and robustness benchmarks. For example, Table 10 reports 0.4–0.6 mIoU gains, while Table A.4 shows consistent improvements across several distribution shifts.

The appendix substantially strengthens the submission through distillation, masking-ratio, loss-weight, and branch-count ablations, together with repeated runs and detailed training recipes. Algorithm 1, Tables B.1–B.2, and the stated code availability support reproducibility. This combination of simplicity and substantial empirical validation supports weak acceptance.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is incremental. The method combines established asymmetric consistency learning, self-distillation, and token masking. In particular, Section 2's distinction between its distillation loss and UDA-style consistency loss is overstated: with a stopped teacher distribution, Equation (3) equals a KL consistency objective plus a teacher-entropy term with zero gradient. The strongest contribution is the effective supervised training recipe and its validation.

The explanation of 'automatic difficulty control' is stronger than the evidence establishes. Figure 2's aggregate gradient curves support the intuition, but Equation (3) does not restrict meaningful masked supervision to correctly predicted examples; a confidently wrong main prediction can still provide a strong target. The reported loss trajectories demonstrate improved optimization without establishing the broader claims about training instability or correctness-dependent difficulty control.

Benefits are not universal, and some headline gains depend on evaluation choices. Table A.10 shows that adding MaskSub during finetuning reduces ViT-B CIFAR-100 accuracy from 91.89% to 89.55%. Section 4.2 explicitly states that best-checkpoint CLIP finetuning accuracy is unchanged, so its reported improvement concerns final-epoch performance. These findings limit the claims of consistently improved performance across settings.

Support is less complete for some peripheral results. The 0.1-point BEiTv2 improvements and GLUE results lack uncertainty estimates, although repeated runs are supplied for several central experiments. Appendix B also omits task-specific GLUE training hyperparameters and metric/selection details. Consequently, these extensions provide weaker evidence than the main ImageNet experiments.

Minor presentation issues include the duplicated CIFAR100 heading in Table 7 and the blanket statement that every experiment uses 50% masking despite BERT using 15%. These are reporting refinements rather than reasons to reject the supported empirical contribution.

strengths: MaskSub provides a simple, technically coherent way to incorporate strong masking into supervised training. The shared-weight model, detached targets, and token-dropping implementation require no additional inference parameters. Its practical simplicity and supported improvements favor weak acceptance.

The central ImageNet results are convincing across strong baselines and model sizes. Table 1 reports gains of 0.6–0.7 percentage points after 400 epochs and 0.3–0.5 after 800 epochs. Three-run results in Table A.13 strengthen this evidence: ViT-B improves from 83.46±0.04 to 84.08±0.02.

The paper meaningfully addresses additional training cost. Table 8 shows ViT-B reaching 84.1% in 25 GPU-days versus 83.7% in 26 GPU-days for longer baseline training. Table 9 also demonstrates a favorable accuracy–cost tradeoff against CoSub, supporting usefulness beyond comparisons at equal epoch counts.

Evaluation breadth is a substantial strength: ResNet, Swin, pretrained-model fine-tuning, downstream recognition, dense prediction, and robustness are covered. ADE20K gains of 0.4–0.6 mIoU and the ViT-B ImageNet-A improvement from 36.8% to 41.9% provide evidence that the benefits extend beyond ImageNet validation accuracy.

The appendix contains meaningful ablations and implementation details. Table A.6 supports the importance of distillation, Tables A.7–A.8 examine masking ratios and loss weights, and repeated runs cover key experiments. Algorithm 1, architecture-specific masking descriptions, detailed training recipes, and a code link support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is incremental. Equation (3) implements consistency between full and masked views using the same model. With detached teacher predictions, cross-entropy and KL divergence produce identical student gradients, so the distinction drawn between MaskSub's distillation loss and UDA's consistency loss does not establish a fundamentally different objective. The strongest contribution is its efficient integration and validation within supervised recipes.

The proposed mechanism is overstated. Equation (3) applies to every sample, including confidently incorrect main-branch predictions; it does not selectively apply masking supervision only to successfully predicted images, as Section 3 suggests. The loss and gradient curves support improved optimization, but do not establish the stronger causal explanation of automatic difficulty control or clearly distinguish training instability from underfitting.

The practical benefits have meaningful exceptions. Adding MaskSub during fine-tuning reduces ViT-B CIFAR-100 accuracy from 91.89% to 89.55% in Table A.10, and several GLUE results decline. Section 4.2 also states that CLIP's best-checkpoint accuracy is unchanged, despite improved final-checkpoint accuracy. These acknowledged limitations warrant narrower claims than improvement in 'all cases.'

Some secondary comparisons provide weaker evidence than the central experiments. Table 6 mixes training recipes and, in one comparison, architectures, limiting attribution of the reported gaps to MaskSub. Small gains such as BEiTv2's 0.1 percentage point lack reported variability. GLUE reproducibility is also limited by the absence of task-specific learning rates, training lengths, and checkpoint-selection details.

The efficiency advantage depends on the architecture. ResNet and Swin retain masked spatial positions and require approximately twice the training computation. Although the ViT budget comparisons and larger-ResNet results are persuasive, they do not establish a general efficiency advantage across all evaluated settings. Separately, Table 7's duplicated CIFAR-100 heading is a minor presentation error; the first dataset is CIFAR-10.

It adds no inference parameters. The practical contribution and supporting experiments favor weak acceptance despite the reservations below.

Improvements over strong supervised baselines are consistent across model scales and training lengths. Table 1 reports gains of 0.3–0.7 percentage points across DeiT-III configurations. Three-run results substantiate key improvements: Table A.13 reports ViT-B increasing from 83.46 ± 0.04 to 84.08 ± 0.02.

The paper meaningfully accounts for additional computation. Table 8 compares 400-epoch MaskSub with 600-epoch standard training: ViT-B achieves 84.1 versus 83.7 accuracy at approximately equal cost, 25 versus 26 GPU days. Table 9 also demonstrates a favorable accuracy–cost tradeoff against CoSub. These comparisons strengthen the case beyond simply spending more computation.

Evaluation breadth is a substantial strength. Experiments cover ResNet, Swin, pretrained-model finetuning, downstream classification, semantic segmentation, detection, and robustness. For example, Table A.4 improves ViT-B ImageNet-A accuracy from 36.8 to 41.9, while Table 10 reports consistent segmentation gains. This supports usefulness beyond ImageNet classification.

The appendix supplies valuable ablations of distillation, masking ratios, loss weights, and multiple branches, alongside repeated runs for several central experiments. Algorithm 1, detailed vision training recipes, and the supplied code link support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is narrower than the framing suggests. With detached teacher predictions, Equation (3) has the same optimization gradient as KL consistency, since CE(p, q) = KL(p || q) + H(p). Consequently, Section 2's distinction between MaskSub's distillation loss and UDA's consistency loss does not establish a fundamentally different objective. The strongest contribution is the effective integration and evaluation of masking within supervised recipes.

The proposed mechanism is only partially established. Figure 2 supports improved optimization, but average gradient norms and loss curves do not demonstrate that masking causes training instability or that MaskSub implements correctness-dependent difficulty control. Equation (3) also propagates confidently incorrect teacher predictions; it contains no correctness gate supporting the statement that augmentation is applied exclusively to successfully learned images. This limits the explanatory claims rather than invalidating the algorithm.

Benefits are broad but not universal. In Table A.10, adding MaskSub during finetuning decreases ViT-B CIFAR-100 accuracy from 91.89 to 89.55 using the same MaskSub-pretrained backbone. Section 4.2 also states that CLIP's best-epoch accuracy is unchanged, so its reported improvement concerns final-epoch performance. These exceptions warrant more analysis before recommending the method as a broadly reliable default.

Statistical support is uneven. Although repeated runs convincingly support the main ViT results, uncertainty is not reported for several smaller gains, including the 0.1-point BEiTv2 improvements and the modest dense-prediction gains. Furthermore, Table 6 mixes training recipes for many self-distillation comparisons; only selected methods are evaluated under RSB. It therefore supports narrower conclusions than the assertion that most existing self-distillation methods are incompatible with strong recipes.

Smaller reporting and reproducibility issues remain: Table A.6 does not clearly specify the objective used in its 'without KD loss' condition, and Appendix B omits task-specific BERT optimization settings. Table 7 also labels both CIFAR columns as CIFAR100. These are correctable documentation issues, not primary reasons for the recommendation.
